Reddit Sinks 6% as Traffic Falls 13% on Google's AI Overviews: "Not Traffic Drivers" ©Brett Jordan from Pexels, Karola G from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Reddit shares fell 6% after Similarweb data showed a 13% drop in global visits, which Business Insider blamed on Google's AI Overviews.

Most of the lost visits were logged out, and the logged-in users behind over 80% of its monetization are still growing.

Pinterest's record user count and Meta's rising ad prices suggest advertisers keep paying for audiences that come back on their own.

Reddit's forward P/E is about half its one-year average, so the AI fear already looks priced in.

Reddit (RDDT:NYSE) is down 6% today after Business Insider reported that its global visits fell 13% from October 2025 to October 2026, according to Similarweb, and blamed Google's AI Overviews.

Two other ad platforms have a stake in this. Pinterest (PINS:NYSE) lists changes at search engines among its own risks. Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) sells ads to the kind of logged-in audience Reddit is now betting on.

The users who pay are still showing up

On Reddit's third-quarter call, CEO Steve Huffman said Google's AI Overviews "are not traffic drivers." U.S. daily active uniques fell to 50.7 million from 53.2 million in the second quarter. All of the drop came from logged-out users, and logged-in U.S. users rose 1% to 23.4 million.

COO Jen Wong said on the call that "over 80% of our monetization sits on the shoulders of logged-in in-app users." Third-quarter revenue rose 53% to $895 million. Analysts expect revenue to keep growing through 2028:

Reddit (RDDT): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2028 (TIKR)

I don't think a count of mostly logged-out visits should make them cut those numbers.

Pinterest and Meta point the same way

Pinterest isn't showing the squeeze yet. Its monthly users hit a record 661 million in the third quarter, up 10%, and users in the U.S. and Canada rose 4% to 107 million. Monthly users aren't visits, though, so its report in early February will show whether Google is costing it traffic too.

Meta shows what logged-in users are worth. Its third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, and its price per ad rose 14%. That's the model Reddit is chasing as it pushes visitors to log in.

Priced for a lot worse

Reddit's forward P/E is close to its low for the past year:

Reddit (RDDT): forward (NTM) P/E, last year (TIKR)

Reddit traded at 12x forward earnings at the last close, against a one-year average of 25x, and today's drop takes it even lower.

Reddit Inc. has seen its share price fall sharply this year, and the slide raises a straightforward question for investors who care about fundamentals. Is the current price tag on Reddit stock supported by what the business is earning today and what those earnings might reasonably deliver over time?

The share price is down 56.3% year to date, which puts the focus squarely on whether that reset lines up with the earnings power that Reddit is currently generating.

Management is pushing users toward a logged-in experience and new ad formats as search referral traffic falls, which can influence how quickly earnings grow and how predictable they become.

Your read on Reddit is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think Reddit's shares could be worth.

For investors, the debate is whether Reddit's latest share price reflects a fair multiple of its earnings given the user trends and monetization plan now in play.

If you are weighing Reddit's sharp year-to-date slide against its earnings story, it can help to compare that setup with other companies that screen as 32 high quality undervalued stocks.

Is Reddit Still Cheap on Earnings?

The P/E ratio fits Reddit because earnings are now positive and investors can at least anchor the share price to a real profit figure. Reddit trades at about 20.6x earnings, which is above the Interactive Media and Services sector average of roughly 9.0x but well below the peer group on about 37.8x.

The tailored fair multiple that blends Reddit's growth profile, margins, size and risks suggests a higher P/E than where the stock trades today, so the current 20.6x screens as undervalued on this framework. Because the sharp pullback followed concerns over slowing user growth and weaker guidance, the discount persists despite those risks already being front of mind for many investors. title: My parents are in their early 60s with no savings, a mortgage, and $2,400 in Social Security: where can they afford to live?
detail:
My parents are in their early 60s with no savings, a mortgage, and $2,400 in Social Security: where can they afford to live?
Christy Bieber
Wed, November 11, 2026 at 4:45 PM MST 6 min read
RDDT
Trade Reddit on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Quick Read

The parents' $500,000 home equity, withdrawn at a safe 3.9% rate, could generate $19,500 annually to supplement their $2,200 Social Security income.

Selling the home risks losing ACA subsidies if income exceeds $84,600, potentially raising health insurance premiums by 114% before Medicare eligibility at 65.

Options beyond selling include a reverse mortgage, an ADU on a child's property, or converting equity into annuities for guaranteed income.

A Reddit poster recently turned to the internet for help with his parents' finances. He fears their retirement is at risk because they have very little saved and can barely cover their everyday bills.

He wants to know where they could realistically live and what concrete moves could give them a measure of security. What follows is the situation the original poster (OP) described, along with the options the couple can weigh to build a more sustainable retirement on limited assets.

fizkes / Shutterstock.com
A workplace injury and a lack of retirement planning left the parents in crisis

According to the OP, his parents did not get far in formal schooling. His father had to stop working on the farm after a back injury left him disabled. A $100,000 settlement helped, but it was not large enough to cover the years until Social Security eligibility, so the couple spent it while waiting to qualify.

The couple now receives a combined $2,200 per month from Social Security. The mother picks up occasional babysitting work, but jobs are scarce in their rural town, and she spent years at home raising children rather than building a career. Without a habit of saving for retirement, they have no nest egg and no pension from the father's former employer.

Their budget is stretched by a $1,500 monthly mortgage and a $300 car payment. Those costs exceed the Social Security income plus the mother's sporadic babysitting pay. The OP is asking whether the couple should sell the home and, if so, where they could move to make their income last as long as possible.

Strategic steps to create a sustainable retirement without savings
Andy Dean Photography / Shutterstock.com

Andy Dean Photography / Shutterstock.comAndy Dean Photography / Shutterstock.com

Selling the house is a logical starting point. The OP estimates the couple holds about $500,000 in home equity while paying a costly mortgage, and a sale would convert that equity into money that can be invested. Morningstar's 2025 State of Retirement Income report, published December 3, 2025, found that 3.9% is the highest safe starting withdrawal rate for retirees who want steady, inflation-adjusted spending over 30 years, assuming a 90% chance the money lasts. That rate rose from 3.7% in the previous year's research. Applied to $500,000, it would yield roughly $19,500 in the first year, which would add to Social Security and free up room in the budget if the couple can find housing for less than the $1,500 they now pay.

Quick Read

At 7% annual growth, $1.3 million compounds to roughly $3.59 million in 15 years, exceeding the $2.56 million needed to generate $100,000 annually.

Stopping contributions forfeits employer match dollars, which represent an immediate 50 to 100 percent return, along with annual tax savings and a cushion against early-retirement market downturns.

A Roth IRA and taxable brokerage account add tax diversification and penalty-free access before age 59½, strengthening long-term retirement resilience beyond the 401(k).

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

A Reddit user recently asked a question that many high-earning savers eventually face: at what point does contributing to a 401(k) stop mattering because compound growth can do most of the work?

The 44-year-old poster has already built a $1.3 million balance and plans to retire at 59 1/2. He noted that even maxing out his contributions would equal just 1% of his account's expected annual growth. His target is at least $100,000 a year in retirement income. Can he coast from here, or does stopping early carry costs he has not counted?

JackF from Getty Images and towfiqu barbhuiya

The answer depends on how much he needs at retirement and what he gives up by stepping back now.

Calculating the retirement target

Before deciding whether to stop, he needs a finish line. How much wealth would produce $100,000 a year without eating into principal?

Morningstar's research now treats the long-standing 4% rule as an unreliable benchmark for new retirees. Its 2025 State of Retirement Income report, published in December 2025, puts the highest safe starting withdrawal rate at 3.9% for retirees who want steady, inflation-adjusted income over a 30-year retirement with a 90% chance of not running out of money. That is up from the 3.7% Morningstar estimated for 2024. The base case assumes a balanced portfolio, and Morningstar's analysis finds that heavier stock weightings lower the safe rate, because added volatility outweighs the extra expected return. Every flexible withdrawal strategy the researchers tested supported a higher starting rate than the 3.9% base case.

Snap Soars 7% as Deutsche Bank Says Its Subscription Story Is "Better Than the Tape Suggests" ©Marcela Ruth Romero from Ruty Romero's Images and mohamed abdelghaffar from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Snap shares rose 7% after Deutsche Bank kept its Buy rating and $8 target, saying investors underrate its subscriptions.

Paid subscribers rose 77% to about 30 million last quarter, bringing in about three-quarters of Snap's added revenue.

Meta Platforms, Pinterest and Reddit all grew revenue far faster than Snap's ads, so the slowdown looks like Snap's own.

The stock looks cheap on forward earnings, though those exclude about $1 billion a year of stock pay.

Snap (SNAP:NYSE) shares are up 7% today, after Deutsche Bank's Benjamin Black argued last week's post-earnings selloff missed what's driving the business. His Nov. 10 note is titled "Better Than the Tape Suggests; Subs Mix and Earnings Power Matter."

Reddit (RDDT:NYSE) is up 7% too. But the note goes straight at Snap's weak spot: its ad business barely grew last quarter, while Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) and Pinterest (PINS:NYSE) kept growing at double-digit rates.

30 million people now pay for Snapchat

Paid subscribers rose 77% to about 30 million in the third quarter, and other revenue, mostly subscriptions, jumped 84% to $350 million. Advertising grew just 4% to $1.37 billion. So subscriptions brought in about three-quarters of the revenue Snap added. Black wrote: "Subscriptions increasingly matter to both the quality of revenue and the margin story, yet we think this remains underappreciated by investors."

Analysts expect revenue to keep climbing through 2028:

Snap (SNAP): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Black sees subscription revenue of about $1.81 billion in 2027, up about 35%, against consensus of roughly 11% growth for the whole company. Gross margin rose from 55.3% a year earlier to 62.3% in the third quarter.

Snap (SNAP): gross margin (%), last 8 quarters (to September 30, 2026) (TIKR)
Snap's ad problem is its own

North American daily users fell 6% to 92 million.

Rivals aren't seeing the same thing. Meta grew third-quarter revenue 26% to $64.6 billion. Pinterest grew 12%. And Reddit grew revenue 53% as its daily users rose 12%. Advertisers are still spending, just less with Snap, which is why subscriptions matter so much.

Cheap, with one big caveat

Black's $8 target is about 60% above Snap's close before today's jump. The stock traded at 6.6x forward earnings at the last close, well under its one-year average of about 12x. But those normalized earnings leave out roughly $1.05 billion of stock pay this year.
